claims.text: The initial equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi powder exhibits a metastable FCC solid solution.
Ti makes CoCrFeNiTi prone to HCP precipitation during thermal exposure.
Six hours of high-energy ball milling generates high-density dislocation networks.
Six hours of milling produces grains smaller than 500 nm.
Milling-induced lattice strain and grain refinement lower the barrier for an FCC-to-BCC transition.
Milling-generated dislocations and grain boundaries act as nucleation sites for the FCC/BCC transition.
Milling-generated grain boundaries inhibit the Ti segregation required for HCP formation.
Atomic-radius mismatch increases stored energy and lattice distortion until BCC becomes thermodynamically favored over FCC.
A VEC of 7.5-8.0 and atomic-radius mismatch below 6.6% favor FCC/BCC coexistence over HCP in CoCrFeNiTi.
SPS at 1000°C supplies sufficient diffusion and pressure-assisted consolidation for densification.
SPS at 1000°C remains below the kinetic threshold for Ti-rich HCP precipitation.
Higher temperatures or longer thermal exposures promote brittle phases in Nb-doped CoCrFeNi alloys.
The proposed process will produce porosity below 2%.
The proposed process will produce a nanocrystalline FCC/BCC dual-phase microstructure.
The processed CoCrFeNiTi alloy will have Vickers hardness above 400 HV.
The processed alloy will have better ductility than single-phase HCP or brittle Laves-phase alloys.
Cast CoCrFeNiTi has hardness below 200 HV.
SPS temperatures above 1050°C cause grain growth or phase decomposition in the proposed CoCrFeNiTi material.
Milling beyond 8 hours causes grain coarsening or nucleation of Ti-rich HCP/Laves phases.
A 50 g Vickers indentation load isolates grain-boundary strengthening from precipitation hardening.

contradictions.description: Using conventional elemental VEC values, equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi has VEC about 7.4, which falls outside the stated maintained window of 7.5-8.0.

The text repeatedly conflates Ti-driven HCP precipitation with Laves-phase formation. Laves phases and HCP solid-solution or precipitate phases are distinct phase categories, so suppressing one does not establish suppression of the other.
